options: Requirement, capability list, architecture sketch, boundary conditions, SOW
Architecture sketch, capability list, requirement, boundary conditions, SOW
Requirement, boundary conditions, capability list, architecture sketch, SOW
Capability list, SOW, architecture sketch, requirement, boundary conditions
questions.explanation: Scoping runs from business requirement to capability list, then architecture sketch assigning owners, then boundary conditions, then the SOW that contains them. Skipping a step produces a commitment that will not survive the next conversation with the business owner.
questions.mnemonic: Need, list, sketch, bounds, SOW.

questions.stem: An architecture handles typed forms reliably but not handwritten ones. Where should that limit be recorded?
options: In the post-launch retrospective report
In the model deprecation runbook
In the system prompt, as an instruction
In the SOW, as a boundary condition
questions.explanation: Boundary conditions state when the architecture works and when it does not, and the SOW contains them so the development team and the business owner both know what is out of scope. Telling the model in a prompt does not record the limit for the people committing to the scope.
questions.mnemonic: Works for some inputs, not others? Write the boundary into the SOW.

questions.stem: Which three inputs form the basis of the monthly cost estimate before any code is written?
options: Number of subagents, hook count and retry limit
Team size, sprint length and delivery route
Call volume, token budget per request, and model tier
Dataset size, embedding dimensions and chunk overlap
questions.explanation: Call volume, token budget per request (input plus expected output) and model tier drive the estimate, with sensitivity analysis on top. The other options are not sizing inputs.
questions.mnemonic: Volume times tokens times tier gives the bill.

questions.stem: A cost model used the average document's token count. After launch, the longest documents consumed most of the token spend. What was the modelling error?
options: Applying output token rates to the input tokens
Choosing the wrong delivery route for the traffic
Ignoring the Batch API discount in the model
Assuming a uniform distribution instead of modelling the tail
questions.explanation: Token distributions are often skewed: a tail of long requests consumes a disproportionate share, so average-based models can underestimate cost by two or three times. Model the distribution, not just the average.
questions.mnemonic: Mean hides the tail; the tail eats the budget.

questions.stem: Why is p95 a better latency design target than the median?
options: SLA breaches are usually caused by the slowest requests at the high end
p95 measures output length in tokens rather than elapsed time
The median is always below the SLA, so it needs no monitoring
Only the slowest 5% of requests can ever exceed the median
questions.explanation: P95 is the value below which 95% of requests complete, and SLA breaches typically come from the slower tail. The median reflects the middle of the pack and hides those breaches.
questions.mnemonic: Breaches live in the tail; design to p95.

questions.stem: A design works only if document length stays under a threshold and the retrieval index is refreshed on a defined schedule. Which verdict is this, and what must be done?
options: Feasible as scoped; state the assumptions only
Feasible with constraints; document each constraint and its failure mode
Feasible as scoped; add a hook to enforce the refresh schedule
Not feasible; end the engagement at this point
questions.explanation: A design that works only under enforced conditions is feasible with constraints, and each constraint must be documented with its failure mode. An undocumented constraint becomes an infeasible system when violated in production.
questions.mnemonic: Works if, so write the ifs down.

questions.stem: At least one capability faces a property limitation that cannot be compensated within scope and budget. What should the verdict document?
options: A list of tools the team might try at a later stage
The expected payback period under optimistic volume assumptions
The disqualifying constraint, and any scope reduction that changes the verdict
Only that the model tier selected was too small
questions.explanation: A not-feasible verdict is a correct assessment that saves a more expensive failure later. State which constraint disqualifies and why, and name a scope reduction that would change it so the business owner can choose.
questions.mnemonic: Not feasible: name the blocker, offer the smaller scope.

questions.stem: Match feasibility questions to properties: which TWO are correct pairings? Select TWO.
options: Knowledge: does the task require choosing a delivery route?
Working memory: is the output schema valid JSON?
Next token prediction: does the task depend on the latency p95?
Steerability: are the instructions specific, concrete and verifiable?
Working memory: do the inputs fit the context window in aggregate?
questions.explanation: Working memory asks whether inputs fit the window; steerability asks whether instructions are specific and verifiable. Knowledge asks whether information is rare, contested or recent, and next-token prediction asks about precision on specific values.
questions.mnemonic: Memory asks fit; steerability asks specific; knowledge asks fresh; tokens ask precision.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes the four-step ROI mapping?
options: Choose the pillars, set the performance SLA, subtract only build cost, then skip sensitivity analysis
Take run cost from the average token cost, subtract the baseline, then quote total revenue as the value of the system
Estimate the baseline from intuition, assume full automation, ignore the run cost, quote one optimistic payback period
Name the baseline in a business unit, predict the post state in that unit, subtract run cost, state payback with sensitivity
questions.explanation: Baseline in a business unit from the owner's operational data, post state in the same unit including human review, subtract the sizing run cost, then state payback with sensitivity. The other options contain the named ROI errors.
questions.mnemonic: Baseline, after, minus run cost, payback with sensitivity.

questions.stem: A value case assumed claims review labour disappears entirely, yet the design includes a human review gate for low-confidence outputs. What happens after launch?
options: Actual analyst hours fall less than the business case promised
The baseline is recalculated automatically by the finance team
Run cost drops well below the sizing model's estimate
The token distribution shifts toward the average request length
questions.explanation: With a human review gate, labour is reduced but not eliminated. Modelling it as eliminated overstates value and surfaces in the first operational period when analyst hours fail to fall as promised.
questions.mnemonic: Review gate means reduced labour, not zero labour.

questions.stem: Which TWO are among the most common ROI map errors? Select TWO.
options: Using the sizing distribution for the run cost
Stating payback with a sensitivity analysis
Taking run cost from an average rather than the distribution
Measuring both states in the same business unit
Estimating the baseline instead of measuring it
questions.explanation: Estimated baselines and average-based run costs both overstate net value, the latter concentrating in heavy-tailed workflows. The other options describe correct practice.
questions.mnemonic: Measured baseline, distributed cost: never guessed, never averaged.

questions.stem: Which list names the five value pillars used to frame an ROI claim?
options: Baseline, projection, run cost, payback, sensitivity
Efficiency, transformation, productivity, solution cost, performance SLAs
Accuracy, safety, latency, scale, compliance
Entry point, interface, route, primitive, pattern
questions.explanation: Efficiency (same work faster or cheaper), transformation (previously infeasible work), productivity (more output from same people), solution cost, and performance SLAs. Each ROI claim should map to the pillar it advances.
questions.mnemonic: E-T-P-C-S: efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, SLAs.

questions.stem: A prototype works well and the business owner is eager to proceed. Why should the architect hold off on confirming feasibility?
options: Feasibility means little until volume and SLA constraints are applied at scale
The model version must be pinned before any verdict can be issued
A delivery route must be chosen before feasibility can be assessed
The ROI payback period must be calculated before feasibility is judged
questions.explanation: 'Technically feasible' is meaningless unless the constraints are applied at the expected scale; confirming feasibility from a working demo before gathering volume and SLA constraints is the trap. ROI mapping follows the feasibility verdict rather than preceding it.
questions.mnemonic: A working demo isn't a verdict: apply the constraints at scale first.

questions.stem: Which TWO constraints must be applied at the expected scale before a use case is confirmed as feasible? Select TWO.
options: Call volume
Team size
SLA latency requirement
Preferred delivery route
Demo pass rate
questions.explanation: Confirming feasibility before gathering the volume and SLA constraints feels efficient, but 'technically feasible' is meaningless until those constraints are applied at the expected scale. A working demo shows capability, not feasibility; team size and the preferred delivery route are not the constraints the verdict rests on.
questions.mnemonic: Volume and SLA at real scale first; a working demo is not a verdict.

questions.stem: A use case is judged feasible as scoped: every capability favors Claude, cost is under the ceiling and p95 is inside the SLA. What must the verdict document?
options: Nothing further, since no compensating control changes the architecture
Each failure mode for every constraint the design could violate
Its assumptions, since changed assumptions can make it feasible with constraints
The scope reduction that would make the verdict not feasible
questions.explanation: A feasible-as-scoped verdict should state its assumptions clearly, because it becomes feasible with constraints when those assumptions change. Documenting each constraint's failure mode belongs to the feasible-with-constraints verdict, and naming a scope reduction belongs to not feasible.
questions.mnemonic: Feasible as scoped stands on assumptions: write them down before they shift.

questions.stem: A design was judged feasible as scoped on the stated assumption that every input arrives in English. The business now wants to add three more languages. How should the verdict be viewed?
options: It still holds, because feasibility was approved at project sign-off
It becomes not feasible automatically, so the project must stop
It must be reassessed, since a stated assumption no longer holds
It is unaffected, because input language is an implementation detail
questions.explanation: A feasible-as-scoped verdict states its assumptions because it changes when they change; the new requirement becomes a documented constraint with its failure mode. Sign-off does not freeze the verdict, a changed assumption does not stop the project automatically, and input language is a scoping assumption, not an implementation detail.
questions.mnemonic: Assumption breaks, verdict reopens: reassess and document the new constraint.

questions.stem: Which of the four AI properties is most often overlooked in a feasibility assessment, and why?
options: Working memory, since small, clean development inputs rarely hit the window
Knowledge, since domain gaps only appear after the model is updated
Steerability, since instructions always look concrete during scoping
Next token prediction, since extraction errors are visible in demos
questions.explanation: Working memory is the most overlooked property because it rarely shows up during development on small, clean inputs, yet it surfaces in production. Skipping any property risks missing a constraint that changes the design.
questions.mnemonic: Memory hides in small demos: working memory bites only at production size.

questions.stem: A multi-document review tool passed every development test on short sample files. In production, requests combining dozens of long documents begin to fail. Which feasibility check was most likely skipped, and what compensates?
options: The knowledge check; fine-tune the model on the document corpus
The steerability check; add more few-shot examples to the prompt
The next token check; raise the sampling temperature for variety
The working memory check; chunking, progressive loading or a pipeline
questions.explanation: When inputs in aggregate exceed the context window, the working memory property applies, compensated by chunking, progressive context loading, summarization across turns or a pipeline architecture. Knowledge and steerability address different limits and would not fix an input that does not fit.
questions.mnemonic: Too much to hold? Chunk it, stage it, pipeline it.

questions.stem: An architect is sizing an invoice-processing workflow before any code is written. Where should the call-volume figure come from?
options: The request count observed in the POC sample dataset
The business owner, based on the business requirement
The developer's estimate, based on similar past projects
The documented rate limit per minute for the model tier
questions.explanation: Call volume comes from the business requirement and the business owner, not from the developer's intuition or a sample dataset. A POC sample reflects demo traffic, not the production figure the cost model needs.
questions.mnemonic: Volume comes from the owner, not the sample or the developer's hunch.

questions.stem: A sizing model is complete except for step four, the sensitivity analysis. Which TWO questions does that step ask? Select TWO.
options: Which model tier did the POC happen to use?
What happens to cost if call volume doubles?
How many engineers are needed to build the system?
What happens if the token distribution shifts toward the tail?
Which vendor has the lowest list price this quarter?
questions.explanation: Sensitivity analysis asks how cost moves if volume doubles or the token distribution shifts toward the tail, revealing how fragile the model is and which assumptions to verify with the business owner. The POC's tier and staffing do not test the model's fragility.
questions.mnemonic: Double the volume, fatten the tail: sensitivity shows where the cost model snaps.

questions.stem: In the four-step ROI mapping, where should the one-off build cost be accounted for?
options: Subtracted with run cost from the monthly operational gain
Folded into the baseline state as a cost of today's process
In the payback period, alongside accumulated gain and run cost
Excluded, since only recurring run cost affects the value case
questions.explanation: Step three subtracts only the recurring run cost taken from the sizing model; build cost is handled separately in step four, where payback is the time for accumulated gain to cover build and run cost. Excluding build cost entirely would overstate the case.
questions.mnemonic: Run cost in step three, build cost in the payback: keep the bills apart.

questions.stem: A value statement reports a net monthly gain and a single payback period of seven months, with nothing further. What is the main weakness?
options: It should report the payback period in tokens rather than months
It omits the latency p95, which belongs in the payback figure
It should use the POC bill as the run cost for accuracy
It lacks sensitivity on how payback shifts if volume or gain assumptions fail
questions.explanation: A payback period should come with sensitivity showing how it moves if volume or gain-per-task assumptions are wrong; a single figure invites decisions on one optimistic scenario. Using the POC bill as run cost would repeat the demo-cost mistake.
questions.mnemonic: One payback number is a wish; payback plus sensitivity is a plan.

questions.stem: A sizing model assumes prompt caching will cut input cost for a long, stable system prompt, but requests arrive only about every 20 minutes. What should the architect expect?
options: Little saving: the default 5-minute TTL expires between requests
Full savings, since caching applies automatically without request markers
Free cache reads, so input cost drops to almost nothing
Larger savings as traffic falls, since fewer writes are needed
questions.explanation: With the default 5-minute cache TTL, workloads whose requests arrive less often than the TTL will not realize consistent caching savings, and cache writes cost more per token than standard input, so the cost model must include the first-use write cost. Caching also needs explicit cache_control markers; it is not automatic.
questions.mnemonic: Cache lives five minutes: sparse traffic keeps paying for writes, never banking savings.
